title: Error Handling Design
learning_outcomes: Explain the central rule or purpose of error handling design using at least one correct term from the lesson.
Interpret or adapt a small Kotlin example that demonstrates error handling design.
Identify one relevant edge case, debugging step, or version/platform constraint.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn **Error Handling Design** as part of **Exceptions, Files, and Input/Output**. Catch or represent expected failures at a boundary where the program can respond usefully; do not silently swallow errors or expose secrets in messages. Use the subtopics—Exceptions Versus Explicit Return Types, Input Validation, Preserving Useful Error Context—as a checklist: predict what the example will do, then verify it in a project configured for the target platform.
content.why_it_matters: Real projects depend on reliable error handling, modular organization, reproducible builds, and safe language boundaries. This lesson helps turn isolated syntax into maintainable applications.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Catch or represent expected failures at a boundary where the program can respond usefully; do not silently swallow errors or expose secrets in messages.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with exceptions versus explicit return types. Then compare it with input validation. Identify the input, state, dependency, or branch that determines the result. The snippet is a static reference for CodeLeaf and is not executed in the lesson page.

items.title: Exceptions Versus Explicit Return Types
items.text: Exceptions Versus Explicit Return Types describes how behavior is declared, passed, or composed. Make inputs and return types clear, keep side effects visible, and use a small call-site example to judge readability.

items.title: Input Validation
items.text: Input Validation defines a trust boundary. Validate untrusted input at the boundary, keep secrets server-side, check authorization where the protected operation occurs, and test both allowed and rejected cases.

items.title: Preserving Useful Error Context
items.text: Preserving Useful Error Context is one part of error handling design. Connect its definition to the example, identify the input/state it changes, and verify the expected behavior with a small test case.

content_blocks.code:
fun parseCount(text: String): Int? = text.toIntOrNull()

fun main() = println(parseCount("not-a-number") ?: "Invalid count")
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save the snippet in a Kotlin/JVM console project and run the configured Gradle application task, or use the Kotlin Playground for examples that need no external dependencies.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the documented starting values, rerun the smallest test, and compare the result with the expected output. If behavior differs, check the compiler/plugin/runtime versions and the active target before changing more than one thing.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Catching every exception and ignoring it is a safe recovery strategy.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the example fails, first confirm which runtime/project type the snippet requires. Read the first useful compiler or runtime message, check imports and declared dependencies, reduce the example to a minimal case, and rerun. For target-specific code, use the target toolchain rather than assuming a console or browser runner can execute it.
